items.title: Why Iran's grip on the Strait of Hormuz runs through Qeshm
items.hook: The US struck Iranian air defences on Qeshm Island on 6 Nov, its second strike there in a week. The island sits at the heart of a strategy Iran built after its naval clashes with the US in the 1980s [[e:Tanker War]].
items.body:
Look at a map and Iran's advantage is obvious. The Strait of Hormuz is only about 35 miles wide at its narrowest, and its northern shore, along with a chain of islands led by **Qeshm**, the largest island in the Gulf, belongs to Iran. Whoever holds those shores can watch, and threaten, every tanker leaving the Gulf. Empires understood this long before oil: the Portuguese seized Hormuz island in the early 1500s, and Persia's Shah Abbas, with English ships, drove them out in the [[e:Capture of Ormuz (1622)|1622 capture of Ormuz]].

The modern story begins with Britain's exit. When London withdrew its forces from the Gulf in 1971, the Shah moved to fill the gap. On the eve of the UAE's founding, Iran took the Greater and Lesser Tunbs by force and Abu Musa under a deal with Sharjah, in the [[e:Seizure of Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs|seizure of the three islands]]. The UAE has disputed them ever since. Iran now held a ring of positions across the shipping lanes.

The 1979 revolution turned that geography against the West, and the [[e:Iran–Iraq War]] {{note: Started when Saddam Hussein's Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980; it ended in a UN-brokered ceasefire in August 1988.}} showed how it could be used. From 1984 Iraq attacked tankers carrying Iranian oil, and Iran hit back at ships serving Iraq's Gulf backers, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia. In this [[e:Tanker War]] some 450 ships were struck. In 1987 Washington agreed to fly the US flag on Kuwaiti tankers and escort them, in [[e:Operation Earnest Will]]. Iran answered with mines and speedboats run by the [[p:Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps]]. {{note: Created by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's decree in May 1979 to defend the revolution, alongside Iran's regular military.}}

The turning point came in April 1988. A mine nearly sank the frigate USS Samuel B. Roberts, and four days later the US Navy struck back in [[e:Operation Praying Mantis]], sinking much of Iran's regular navy in a single day. That July, the cruiser USS Vincennes mistook a passenger jet for an attacker and shot down [[e:Iran Air Flight 655]], killing all 290 aboard. Iran accepted a ceasefire weeks later.

Tehran drew a lasting lesson: it could not win a ship-against-ship battle with America, but it could make the strait too dangerous to use. Over the following decades the [[p:Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy|Guards' navy]] built up mines, fast attack craft and anti-ship missiles, many dug into tunnels on islands like Qeshm, and took the lead role in the strait. It seized tankers in the 2019 crisis to show it could.

The 2026 war tested that strategy for real. After US–Israeli strikes began on 28 February, Iran shut the strait, and Washington answered with the [[e:2026 United States naval blockade of Iran|naval blockade of Iran]]. The new US strikes on Qeshm's air defences hit the core of the system Iran spent 35 years building, which is why each one risks wider fighting even as both sides talk.

timeline.text: Safavid Persia and the English East India Company expel the Portuguese from Hormuz island.
As Britain leaves the Gulf, Iran takes Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs; the UAE still claims them.
The [[e:Tanker War]] begins inside the Iran–Iraq War; some 450 ships are hit by 1988.
The US begins escorting reflagged Kuwaiti tankers in [[e:Operation Earnest Will]].
After a mine hits USS Samuel B. Roberts, [[e:Operation Praying Mantis]] sinks much of Iran's regular navy.
USS Vincennes shoots down [[e:Iran Air Flight 655]], killing 290; Iran accepts a ceasefire weeks later.
War begins on 28 Feb; Iran closes the strait and the US imposes a [[e:2026 United States naval blockade of Iran|naval blockade]].
US strikes hit air defences on Qeshm on 2 and 6 Nov while indirect talks continue.

perspectives.view: Tehran tells this as a story of foreign powers, from the Portuguese to the US Navy, trying to dominate waters on its doorstep. It sees control of the strait as legitimate self-defence and its only real leverage against a stronger enemy and its blockade.
Washington frames its role since 1987 as protecting freedom of navigation for the world's oil supply. It casts mining and tanker attacks as illegal threats to neutral shipping that it must deter.

The UAE describes the 1971 island takeover as an occupation of its territory on the eve of independence. Gulf states want the strait open but fear being caught in a US–Iran war fought along their coasts.

keyTerms.meaning: Iran's largest island, lying along the strait's northern side; it hosts Revolutionary Guard naval and air-defence sites.
The Revolutionary Guards' naval force, built around mines, fast boats and coastal missiles, which leads Iran's operations in the strait.
Registering foreign ships under a country's flag so its navy can protect them, as the US did for Kuwaiti tankers in 1987.
The principle that ships may pass through international straits; the US invokes it, while Iran disputes how it applies in the 2026 war.

items.whyItMatters: Iran's whole Hormuz strategy rests on islands like Qeshm, so US strikes there weaken Tehran's main bargaining chip and also risk a wider fight. The 1988 record shows such clashes can escalate fast, and one mistake can kill civilians. Watch whether the Qatari-mediated sequence of steps reopens the strait before more strikes hit the islands.

items.recallQ: Why did Iran build its naval strategy in the strait around mines, fast boats and island missile sites rather than a large conventional fleet?
items.recallA: In April 1988, Operation Praying Mantis showed that Iran's regular navy could not survive a direct fight with the US Navy. The Revolutionary Guards concluded that cheap, scattered, hard-to-hit weapons could make the strait too dangerous to use, giving Iran leverage without winning a sea battle.

items.title: How Serbia's students ended the Vučić era
items.hook: Final results confirmed on 5 Nov that the Student List won a clear majority in Serbia's parliament, ending more than a decade of [[p:Aleksandar Vučić]]'s dominance. It is the second time in 26 years that a student-led movement has brought down a Serbian strongman, and the first did not end the way its heroes hoped.
items.body:
Serbia has toppled a strongman with students in the streets once before. In the late 1990s [[p:Slobodan Milošević]] ruled a country battered by the [[e:Yugoslav Wars]], sanctions and hyperinflation. A dozen students in Belgrade founded [[p:Otpor]], {{note: Founded in Belgrade on 10 October 1998 by a small group of students, using a clenched-fist logo and street humour against Milošević.}} a leaderless movement built on mockery, discipline and nonviolence. When Milošević tried to deny [[p:Vojislav Koštunica]] victory in the September 2000 presidential vote, hundreds of thousands converged on Belgrade, and on 5 October he fell in the [[e:Overthrow of Slobodan Milošević|Bulldozer Revolution]].

The democrats who replaced him disappointed many. Reformist prime minister [[p:Zoran Đinđić]] was shot dead by a sniper linked to organised crime and former security units in the [[e:Assassination of Zoran Đinđić|2003 assassination]], and the governments that followed became associated with patronage, privatisation scandals and the 2008 financial crash.

That opening was seized by men from Milošević's own camp. In 1998–2000 [[p:Aleksandar Vučić]] had been Milošević's information minister, a hardline member of the nationalist [[p:Serbian Radical Party]]. In 2008 he and [[p:Tomislav Nikolić]] broke away to found the [[p:Serbian Progressive Party]], {{note: Founded on 8 September 2008 by Nikolić and Vučić as a pro-EU split from the Serbian Radical Party.}} recasting themselves as pro-European reformers. The SNS came to power in 2012; Vučić became prime minister in 2014 and president in 2017.

Over the next decade critics, and watchdogs such as Freedom House, described a slide toward a hybrid regime: friendly tabloids and TV channels, pressure on independent media, public jobs tied to party loyalty, and elections that were competitive but tilted. Vučić's supporters pointed instead to growth, foreign investment, big infrastructure projects and a careful balance between the EU, Russia and China. Protest waves came and went, in 2018–19 and after two mass shootings in 2023, but the fragmented opposition parties could never turn them into a majority.

The break came on 1 November 2024, when the newly renovated concrete canopy of Novi Sad's railway station collapsed in the [[e:Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse]], {{note: The canopy fell on 1 November 2024; the death toll eventually reached 16.}} killing 16 people. For many Serbians the renovation, part of a Chinese-built rail project, symbolised a state where contracts mattered more than safety. Students began blockading their faculties that month, and the [[e:2024–present Serbian anti-corruption protests|movement]] spread to farmers, teachers and lawyers. Like Otpor, it refused to have leaders or to merge with the old opposition. Prime minister [[p:Miloš Vučević]] resigned in January 2025, and on 15 March independent counters estimated around 300,000 people in Belgrade, one of the largest rallies in Serbia's history.

The students then made a decisive choice: instead of backing existing parties, they fielded their own slate of professors, doctors and professionals, the Student List. After Vučić stepped down as president in September 2026 to run for prime minister, the snap election of 25 October became a referendum on his era, and the students won 140 of 250 seats on the highest turnout in three decades.

timeline.text: Students in Belgrade found [[p:Otpor]], a leaderless nonviolent movement against Milošević; the same year Vučić becomes his information minister.
Mass protests over a stolen presidential election topple Milošević in the [[e:Overthrow of Slobodan Milošević|Bulldozer Revolution]].
Reformist PM Zoran Đinđić is assassinated in Belgrade, a blow to the post-Milošević reform project.
Vučić and Nikolić found the [[p:Serbian Progressive Party]] as a pro-EU split from the Radicals; it wins power in 2012.
Vučić becomes prime minister (2014), then president (2017); he is re-elected in 2022.
The [[e:Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse]] kills 16 people and sparks student blockades across Serbia.
PM Miloš Vučević resigns; on 15 March an estimated 300,000 people rally in Belgrade.
After Vučić quits the presidency to run for PM, the Student List wins 140 of 250 seats; final results are confirmed on 5 Nov.

perspectives.view: They present their years in power as a period of stability, growth and investment after the chaotic democratic governments of the 2000s, with Serbia steering its own course between the EU, Russia and China. They have often cast the protests as a foreign-backed attempt at a [[e:Colour revolution|colour revolution]] rather than a genuine domestic movement.

perspectives.side: The student movement and its supporters
perspectives.view: They see the Novi Sad collapse as the deadly result of a captured state, where party loyalty and opaque contracts replaced accountability. In their telling, they are finishing the job of 2000, which removed Milošević but not the system of patronage that let his former officials return.

keyTerms.meaning: Srpska napredna stranka, the [[p:Serbian Progressive Party]]; founded in 2008 and in power from 2012 until the 2026 election.
Serbian for 'Resistance!'; the 1998–2000 student movement whose nonviolent tactics helped topple Milošević and were later copied abroad.
The students' main tactic since November 2024: occupying faculties and roads to halt normal life and press their demands for accountability.
A system that holds real elections but tilts the field through control of media, state resources and institutions; the label watchdogs applied to Serbia under the SNS.

items.whyItMatters: The history of 2000 is the warning: a street victory followed by infighting and weak institutions let the old guard return within a decade. Watch whether the leaderless Student List can agree on a prime minister and hold together once the new assembly sits, how it handles the presidential election due by 27 Dec, and whether it reopens the stalled EU accession track while managing Serbia's ties with Russia and China.

items.title: Why Moscow's choice of Medinsky matters: Russia–Ukraine talks from Minsk to Abu Dhabi
items.hook: Russia is sending [[p:Vladimir Medinsky]] to this week's Abu Dhabi talks, and analysts read that as a sign of stalling. The reason lies in a decade of negotiations that keep producing prisoner swaps and local truces, but never a settlement.
items.body:
Russia and Ukraine have been negotiating, on and off, for more than a decade, and the pattern repeats: talks produce humanitarian deals, but never a settlement, because the two sides disagree about what comes first.

The template was set in Donbas. After Russian-backed separatists seized parts of eastern Ukraine in 2014, the [[e:Minsk agreements]] {{note: Minsk I was signed in September 2014 and Minsk II in February 2015, brokered by France and Germany with Russia and Ukraine.}} promised a ceasefire, local elections and special status for the breakaway areas. They foundered on **sequencing**: Kyiv wanted Russian forces out and its border back before any vote, while Moscow insisted on elections first. Eight years of the [[p:Normandy Format]] {{note: Leaders' grouping of Germany, France, Russia and Ukraine, first convened during D-Day commemorations in Normandy in June 2014.}} never closed that gap. On 21 February 2022 Russia recognised the separatist republics, and Putin declared Minsk dead the next day.

Within days of the [[e:Russian invasion of Ukraine|full-scale invasion]], delegations met in Belarus, and in late March 2022 they reached a draft framework in Istanbul: Ukrainian neutrality in exchange for international security guarantees, with Crimea parked for 15 years. Russia's chief negotiator was [[p:Vladimir Medinsky]] {{note: Russian culture minister from 2012 to 2020 and a presidential aide since 2020; author of popular, nationalist-tinged books on Russian history.}}. Why those [[e:Peace negotiations in the Russo-Ukrainian war (2022–present)|Istanbul talks]] collapsed is still argued over. Moscow says Western leaders talked Kyiv out of a deal. Ukrainian officials say Russia demanded caps on Ukraine's army and a veto over its guarantees, terms they saw as capitulation, and the discovery of the [[e:Bucha massacre]] after Russia's retreat from Kyiv hardened opinion. Many historians point to several causes at once.

The direct channel stayed closed for three years. When it reopened in Istanbul in May 2025, under pressure from the new Trump administration, Moscow sent Medinsky again. The rounds yielded the war's largest prisoner swaps but no ceasefire; Medinsky reportedly reminded Kyiv that Peter the Great fought Sweden for 21 years, a signal that Russia was prepared to wait.

In 2026 the US moved the talks into a trilateral format brokered by [[p:Steve Witkoff]]. Tellingly, Russia changed its negotiator: the two [[e:2026 United States–Ukraine–Russia meetings in Abu Dhabi|Abu Dhabi rounds]] in January and February were led by the military intelligence chief [[p:Igor Kostyukov]], and produced a 314-prisoner exchange and talk of ceasefire mechanics. When Medinsky returned at [[e:2026 United States–Ukraine–Russia meetings in Geneva|Geneva]] in February, the military track was constructive but the political talks stalled again over Russia's demand for all of Donbas. In March the US–Iran war put the format on pause; prisoner swaps carried on through mediators.

That history explains why the choice of Medinsky for this week's Abu Dhabi round is read as a sign. With him at the table, Russia has tended to restate its full political demands rather than trade on details. Ukraine's lead, [[p:Rustem Umerov]], was in the room with him in Istanbul in 2022 and 2025 and in Geneva.

timeline.text: The [[e:Minsk agreements|Minsk Protocol]] sets out a ceasefire in Donbas; it soon breaks down.
Minsk II, brokered by France and Germany, sets out elections and special status for the separatist areas, but the order of steps is never agreed.
Russia recognises the separatist republics, declares Minsk void and launches the [[e:Russian invasion of Ukraine|full-scale invasion]].
Talks in Istanbul, with [[p:Vladimir Medinsky]] leading Russia's team, produce a draft on neutrality and guarantees; they collapse by May.
Direct talks resume in Istanbul under US pressure, again led by Medinsky. They bring large prisoner swaps but no ceasefire.
US-brokered trilateral rounds in Abu Dhabi, led for Russia by GRU chief [[p:Igor Kostyukov]], bring a prisoner swap; at Geneva in February Medinsky returns and political talks stall.
The US–Iran war puts the trilateral format on pause; prisoner exchanges continue through mediators.
The Oleshky local truce lapses on 1 Nov; talks resume in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 Nov with Medinsky facing [[p:Rustem Umerov]].

perspectives.view: Moscow says Kyiv sabotaged the Minsk agreements and walked away from a near-deal in Istanbul in 2022 under Western pressure. It argues any settlement must address the war's 'root causes': Ukraine's NATO ambitions and the status of territories it now claims.

Kyiv says Russia used Minsk to freeze its occupation of Donbas and offered terms in 2022 that would have left Ukraine disarmed and without real guarantees. It wants a ceasefire on current lines first, and refuses to hand over land Russia has not taken.
Many see no single cause for the 2022 collapse, pointing to disputes over guarantees and army limits, Russian atrocities, and shifts on the battlefield. They disagree on how close a deal really was.

keyTerms.meaning: The 2014 and 2015 deals meant to end the war in Donbas. They failed largely over whether elections or Ukraine regaining its border should come first.
The March 2022 draft framework that traded Ukrainian neutrality for security guarantees from other states. It was never finalised.
US–Russia–Ukraine talks, run since January 2026 with American envoys mediating in the room, rather than the bilateral Istanbul channel.
Ukraine's eastern Donetsk and Luhansk regions. Russia's demand for all of it, including areas Ukraine still holds, is the main sticking point.

items.whyItMatters: Past rounds led by Medinsky have restated Russia's maximal political terms, while rounds led by military officials have produced practical deals such as prisoner swaps and ceasefire mechanics. Watch whether Abu Dhabi yields anything beyond humanitarian steps, such as a renewed local truce, and whether talk of territory moves at all. Washington's push for a broader US–Russia deal could also change what each side thinks it can hold out for.

items.recallQ: What was the core 'sequencing' dispute that sank the Minsk agreements, and how does it echo in today's talks?
items.recallA: Ukraine wanted Russian forces withdrawn and its border restored before local elections in Donbas, while Russia insisted elections and special status come first. Today the same gap appears as Kyiv seeking a ceasefire first and Moscow demanding political and territorial terms first.
